pages.text: It was a hot summer afternoon, but the woods were cool and green. A shallow stream ran between the trees. In one place it slowed down into a wide, quiet pool. Rani’s father sat on the bank with a book. Every few lines, he looked up at the water. Celine and Rani had brought their toy animals.
pages.speech: It was a hot summer afternoon, but the woods were cool and green. A shallow stream ran between the trees. In one place it slowed down into a wide, quiet pool. Rani’s father sat on the bank with a book. Every few lines, he looked up at the water. Celine and Rani had brought their toy animals.

pages.text: “Let’s build a raft,” said Rani. “Then the animals can cross the pool.” “Yes,” said Celine. “It needs a tall sail, so the wind can push it.” “No,” said Rani. “It needs a wide, flat floor, so it doesn’t tip.” “A sail,” said Celine. “A floor,” said Rani.

pages.text: They glared at each other. “Fine,” said Celine. “I’ll build my own.” “Fine,” said Rani. “So will I.” They turned their backs and built, crossly, on two sides of a big rock. A dragonfly hovered between them, as if it could not decide whose side to be on.

pages.text: Celine tied two sticks together with a long blade of grass. In the middle she pushed in a tall twig, and on top she fixed her paper napkin. It looked like a real ship. She put her toy rabbit on board and set the raft down on the water.

pages.text: The raft wobbled. The sail leaned. Then the whole thing tipped over, plop, and the rabbit fell into the water. Celine fished him out with a long stick. He was dripping. “It tipped,” she said in a small voice.

pages.text: On the other side of the rock, Rani laid six sticks side by side and tied them with grass. His raft was wide and flat. He put his toy bear on board and pushed it out. It floated beautifully, without a wobble. But it did not go anywhere. It just turned, slowly, in a circle. “It turned,” said Rani.

pages.text: Celine sat down on the bank. Rani sat down on the bank too, but not very close. Nobody said anything. The dragonflies zipped up and down the pool. Rani’s father turned a page, glanced at them over his glasses, and went on reading.

pages.text: Then Rani said, “Tell me about your sail.” Celine looked at him. “The wind pushes it,” she said. She held up the damp napkin by two corners, and the breeze puffed it out into a little round sail. “See?” Rani watched it tug at her fingers.

pages.text: “A flat raft…” said Rani. “With a sail!” said Celine. They laughed. “But not too tall,” said Rani. “And not too small,” said Celine. They shook hands on it, very seriously, like two ship captains.

pages.text: Rani held his wide floor steady. Celine tore her napkin in half and pushed a short twig into the middle of the floor. Together they fixed the half napkin to the twig, and Rani tied it tight with grass. Now the raft was wide and flat, with a small sail standing up straight.

pages.text: Who would be the first passenger? Not the wet rabbit, and not the sleepy bear. They chose the toy hedgehog, because he was the bravest. Together they set the raft down on the water. A breeze came through the trees. The little sail filled.

pages.text: And the raft moved. Slowly and steadily, without a wobble, it sailed out across the pool. Two dragonflies flew beside it. Celine held her breath, and so did Rani. The hedgehog sailed all the way to the other side and bumped gently against a stone. “It sailed,” whispered Celine.

pages.text: They cheered and ran round over the little wooden bridge to fetch it. Rani’s father put down his book and clapped. “What’s your raft called?” he asked. Celine and Rani looked at each other. “Two Ideas,” said Rani. “One Raft,” said Celine.

activity.title: The Paper Bridge
activity.goal: Discover that folding paper makes it stronger.
materials: Two books of the same height

steps.caption: Lay a flat sheet across two books.
Guess first. Then add pebbles, one by one.
Fold a new sheet into a zigzag.
Agree on your bridge. Test again.
Which held more? Count them back.

activity.safety: Pebbles and coins never go in the mouth. Count them all back into a cup at the end, and wash hands afterwards. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Celine and Rani each have a good idea, a sail that moves the raft and a floor that keeps it steady, but each idea fails alone. They stop arguing when each one asks the other to explain, and together they make a raft that neither could make alone. This activity asks two children to do the same with a real problem: how to make a sheet of paper hold more weight. Lay two books of the same height a hand’s width apart and put a flat sheet of paper across them. Before adding anything, both children guess how many pebbles or coins it will hold. Add them one at a time to the middle of the paper and count until the bridge sags and they slide off. Then fold a new sheet back and forth into a zigzag, like a fan. Here is the rule from the story: the pair must agree on one design before testing. They may disagree about how wide the folds should be, and that is the point. Encourage each child to ask the other, “Tell me about your idea,” before they choose. Test the zigzag bridge in the same way and compare the two counts. The folds make the paper much stiffer, so it usually holds many more. Ask them to explain why they think it worked. Praise the listening and the testing (“you tried both ideas”), not being “clever”. To make it easier, the adult folds the zigzag and the children test it. To make it harder, try narrow and wide folds, or roll the paper into a tube. At the end, count every coin back into the cup together.
activity.inClass: Pairs, one bridge each. Each pair must agree on one folded design before testing, and write their guess and their result on a slip of paper. At the end, the class lines up the zigzag bridges, compares the results, and talks about which folds worked best. The teacher counts all the coins or pebbles back in.
